transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, thank you, doctor. I, uh, I really appreciate you seeing me. You see, the main thing, the reason I finally made this appointment—and my supervisor actually made a comment about it the other day too, which was embarrassing, honestly—is that I just... I cannot seem to keep my mind on one single thing anymore. It's like my brain is just constantly jumping around. 

I work at a logistics warehouse, doing freight and inventory counting, and I’ve been doing this kind of work for a while now, so I know the drill, you know? I even took some business classes back in the day, so I understand how important the logistics side is. But lately, I'll be in the middle of a physical count in aisle four, scanner and clipboard in hand, and suddenly... a forklift alarm goes off two aisles over, and my head just snaps to it. Or someone is moving a heavy wooden pallet, and the sound of the wood scraping or the pallet jack pumping up just completely pulls me off my count. 

And it's not just a little distraction where you look up and look back down. It's like I completely lose the thread of what I was doing. I’ll be staring at a shelf, trying to focus, and then a scanner beeper goes off across the floor, and my attention is just gone. By the time I look back at my sheet, I realize I’ve put completely wrong numbers into the inventory log. I mean, putting the wrong numbers in inventory is a huge deal, it messes up the shipping manifests, the supply chain, the next shift's pulls, everything. And I try to focus, I really do, I tell myself, just count these boxes, but every single little noise or movement just drags my attention away, and I just can't stop it from happening, which is why I'm here, because I can't afford to lose this job over something like a messed up pallet count, you know?

Thinking back, did you have similar problems with getting easily distracted and losing focus when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that's really only started more recently as an adult?

No, no, not at all, nothing like this when I was younger. I mean, sure, I was a normal kid, maybe daydreamed a bit in class, but nothing that ever caused problems, certainly not like this. I was always able to buckle down and study, even when I took those business classes at the community college a few years back. I could sit in the library for hours and just focus. 

This whole... scattered feeling, this complete inability to block out the world around me, it’s really just started recently. I’d say it’s been going on for about a month now. And, you know, it’s funny you ask about the timing, because I’ve been trying to figure out what changed, right? Why now? And the only thing I can think of is that it started right around the time my husband, Tom, stopped working outside the home. 

He used to work down at the auto body shop, had been there for twenty years, but his back finally gave out, so now he’s home all day. And it completely threw off our routine. I mean, we had our mornings down to a science—coffee at 5:30, out the door by 6:15, home by 4:00, dinner at 6:00. But now... he’s there when I wake up, he’s there when I get home, the house is just... different. It's not that I don't love having him around, but the whole rhythm of my life has shifted. And it seems like ever since that shift, ever since he's been home and our schedule got turned upside down about a month ago, my brain just decided it couldn't hold onto a single thought anymore. It's like the change in routine just broke my concentration completely.
Since your husband started staying home a month ago, have you noticed yourself feeling persistently anxious, worried, or down about this change, beyond just the distraction at work?

Well, that's the strange part, honestly. You'd think I'd be stressed out or depressed with the whole routine being thrown off and him being hurt, but it's actually... it's almost the opposite, sometimes? I mean, I don't feel down at all. In fact, some days I wake up and I feel just incredibly... energized. Like, almost too upbeat, if that makes sense? 

Just the other day, I woke up at 4:30 in the morning—didn't even need the alarm—and I felt this rush, like I could completely reorganize the garage, fix the loose hinges on the kitchen cabinets, and still go into the warehouse and completely revamp their whole bin-sorting system before dinner. I just felt fantastic, like my mind was firing on all cylinders, even if it couldn't stick to one thing. 

But the problem is, it's a double-edged sword. Because I'll be in that zone, feeling like I can take on the world, and then Tom will come into the kitchen and just ask a simple question, like, "Honey, are you sure we need to pull everything out of the cabinets right now?" And I just... I snap. I mean, I completely bite his head off over nothing. I get so irritable, so fast, just because he's questioning my plan or slowing me down. And then I feel terrible about it later, because I know his back hurts and he's just trying to understand what I'm doing, but in the moment, I just have zero patience. It's like I'm running at a hundred miles an hour and if anyone steps in front of me, I just explode at them. So no, not down or worried, really, just... this weird mix of feeling on top of the world and then getting furiously annoyed at the drop of a hat.

Have you ever had a period before this—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually high, energetic, or irritable like this, or on the other end, a stretch of time where you felt deeply depressed or lost interest in things?

Well, um... no, not that I can recall. I mean, sure, I've had good days and bad days, just like anybody else, right? You know, you get a good night's sleep, the weather is nice, maybe you find a twenty-dollar bill in an old coat pocket, and you feel great for a few days. Or, on the flip side, you get a bad cold, or work is stressful, or, I don't know, the car breaks down—like when the transmission went out on our old Honda Civic back in 2018, that was a nightmare, let me tell you, we were stressed for weeks over the repair bill—but that's just life, isn't it? 

I've never had anything like this, where it lasts for a whole week and I'm just buzzing out of my skin, wanting to tear apart the garage and rebuild it from scratch at four in the morning. And as for feeling deeply depressed or losing interest in things... no, not really. I mean, I've always been a pretty steady person. I like my routine, I like going to work, coming home, watching a little TV with Tom—we usually watch those home renovation shows, they're so relaxing, though lately I just want to jump through the screen and do the renovations myself, faster and better than they do—but no, I've never just stopped caring or felt so low I couldn't get out of bed for a week. 

It's really just been this past month, ever since Tom's back gave out and he had to stop working at the auto body shop. That's when this whole rollercoaster started, this feeling of being totally scattered at the warehouse, but also having these bursts of crazy energy and then snapping at him over nothing. Before this, I was just... normal. Just going about my business, doing my inventory counts, living my life. So, no, I don't think I've ever had a period like you're describing before this whole mess started.

During this past month of feeling so energetic and wired, have you experienced anything like hearing voices or seeing things that others don't, or had any beliefs about yourself—like having special powers or abilities—that others found unrealistic or hard to believe?

Well, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm energetic, sure, and I feel like I can get a million things done, but I'm not crazy. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. I mean, the only voices I hear are the guys at the warehouse yelling over the forklifts, or Tom asking me where the remote is, which, honestly, is annoying enough on its own right now without adding imaginary voices to the mix. 

And as for special powers, well... I mean, I guess I feel like I have a superpower when it comes to organizing right now, because I can look at a messy shelf and just instantly know exactly how it should be arranged for maximum efficiency. Like, I completely reorganized the entire fastener aisle at work on Tuesday. Took me three hours, but it's perfect now. Every nut, bolt, and washer is exactly where it needs to be. But that's just me being good at my job, you know? It's not like I think I can fly or read minds or anything ridiculous like that. I'm just... really, really focused on fixing things right now. Well, focused on fixing things, but not focused enough to actually finish fixing them before I move on to the next thing, if that makes sense. 

But no, no hallucinations or delusions or whatever you call them. I'm just a normal person who suddenly has entirely too much energy and a husband who is always in the way. I mean, just yesterday, I was trying to explain to him how we could completely redesign the backyard landscaping to be drought-tolerant and low-maintenance—because, you know, water bills are getting ridiculous, and with him not working, we need to save where we can—and he just looked at me like I had two heads. He was like, "Honey, it's 9:00 PM, and we don't even own a shovel." But I didn't think I had special powers to do it, I just knew I *could* do it if I had the right tools. So, yeah, no voices, no superpowers. Just a lot of ideas.

Has this level of energy and distractibility actually caused significant problems at work—like disciplinary warnings, mistakes needing correction, or conflicts with coworkers or supervisors—beyond just feeling scattered?

Well, yes, actually. It... it has been causing some real issues, more than just me feeling a bit all over the place. At work, for instance, the warehouse... well, like I said, I've been getting these bursts where I think I'm being incredibly efficient, right? Like with the fastener aisle. But the problem is, because I'm moving so fast and my brain is just jumping from one bin to the next, I've actually messed up some of the inventory counts. And in my line of work, if the counts are off, it throws everything off for the pickers and the shipping department. 

So, last Thursday, my supervisor, Dave—who is usually a pretty laid-back guy, honestly, he’s been there for like fifteen years and nothing really fazes him—he actually had to pull me aside. He showed me this whole list of discrepancies in the sections I’d logged that morning. I had logged a shipment of hex bolts as carriage bolts, and I completely skipped over a whole pallet of washers because I got distracted trying to reorganize the shelving unit next to it. So now, I’m having to double-check everything with him. I literally have to take my logs to Dave before I can enter them into the system, which is just humiliating, honestly. I've been doing this job for a long time, and having to be micromanaged like that because I'm making stupid mistakes... it's really frustrating. But I just can't seem to slow down enough to catch the errors myself.

And then, on top of all that, things at home are just... tense. Really tense. With Tom being home all the time now because of his back, you'd think we'd be settling into this new routine, maybe treating it a bit like an early retirement, you know? Finding a rhythm. But instead, we are just constantly at each other's throats. Well, mostly me at his throat, if I'm being honest. Like I mentioned before, I just snap at him. We’ve been arguing so much over the smallest things—like him asking about the cabinets, or the landscaping ideas, or even just what we’re having for dinner. It's gotten to the point where it feels like we’re just walking on eggshells around each other. He’s trying to stay out of my way because he doesn't know when I'm going to explode, and I'm just irritated that he's even in the room breathing too loudly while I'm trying to figure out how to rewire the toaster. It's exhausting. It's not how I want us to be spending this time together at all, but I just can't seem to turn off this... this motor inside me that gets so aggravated when things aren't moving at my speed. So, yeah, it's definitely causing problems. Big ones.
Over this past month, have you noticed that you need much less sleep than usual—like feeling fully rested after only a few hours—without feeling tired the next day?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know I said earlier about wanting to rebuild the garage at four in the morning, but that’s more just... me lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling fan, with my brain just racing and going over the blueprints in my head while I’m *trying* to sleep. It’s not like I actually function well if I only get a few hours. Goodness, no. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am absolutely dragging the next day. 

I've always been a real stickler for my sleep schedule, you know? Usually, I'm in bed by 10:00 PM, right after the local news—we always watch Channel 5 because Tom likes the weatherman, Greg, he says he's the only one who doesn't exaggerate the rain forecasts—and I usually sleep right through until my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM for work. Lately, though, with Tom tossing and turning so much because of his back pain, he keeps waking me up. He shifts around trying to get comfortable, the mattress squeaks, and then I'm awake. And once I'm awake, that motor just starts humming again and I can't shut it off. 

But I definitely still *need* the sleep. If I only get three or four hours because of all the tossing and turning, I feel like absolute garbage the next morning. I'm yawning all through my shift, having to drink three or four cups of that awful, burnt breakroom coffee just to keep my eyes open while I'm trying to go over my inventory logs with Dave. Even with all this weird, buzzy energy I've been having, my body still physically demands a full night's rest. If I don't get it, I might still be moving fast and snapping at people, but underneath it all, I'm just completely wiped out. So, no, I definitely don't feel fully rested on just a few hours. I wish I did, honestly, because I could get so much more done around the house, but no, I definitely still need my sleep.

I mean, I guess I feel like I have a superpower when it comes to organizing right now, because I can look at a messy shelf and just instantly know exactly how it should be arranged for maximum efficiency. Like, I completely reorganized the entire fastener aisle at work on Tuesday. Took me three hours, but it's perfect now. Every nut, bolt, and washer is exactly where it needs to be. But that's just me being good at my job, you know? It's not like I think I can fly or read minds or anything ridiculous like that. I'm just... really, really focused on fixing things right now. Well, focused on fixing things, but not focused enough to actually finish fixing them before I move on to the next thing, if that makes sense. 

But no, no hallucinations or delusions or whatever you call them. I'm just a normal person who suddenly has entirely too much energy and a husband who is always in the way. I mean, just yesterday, I was trying to explain to him how we could completely redesign the backyard landscaping to be drought-tolerant and low-maintenance—because, you know, water bills are getting ridiculous, and with him not working, we need to save where we can—and he just looked at me like I had two heads. He was like, "Honey, it's 9:00 PM, and we don't even own a shovel." But I didn't think I had special powers to do it, I just knew I *could* do it if I had the right tools. So, yeah, no voices, no superpowers. Just a lot of ideas.

inference.note: Patient denies hallucinations, delusions, or psychotic-level grandiosity, ruling out psychotic features (F30.2) and reinforcing F30.1 (mania without psychotic symptoms) as the leading diagnosis, with F30.9 retained as a less specific alternative.

doctor.intent: Assess degree of functional impairment to determine if symptoms meet threshold for a manic episode (marked disruption of work/social functioning) versus a milder presentation
doctor.question: Has this level of energy and distractibility actually caused significant problems at work—like disciplinary warnings, mistakes needing correction, or conflicts with coworkers or supervisors—beyond just feeling scattered?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had to double-check with my supervisor after making inventory errors, and at home my husband and I have been arguing enough that it feels like we’re walking around each other instead of settling into his retirement.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms have caused significant problems or impairment at work, which maps directly to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. It... it has been causing some real issues, more than just me feeling a bit all over the place. At work, for instance, the warehouse... well, like I said, I've been getting these bursts where I think I'm being incredibly efficient, right? Like with the fastener aisle. But the problem is, because I'm moving so fast and my brain is just jumping from one bin to the next, I've actually messed up some of the inventory counts. And in my line of work, if the counts are off, it throws everything off for the pickers and the shipping department. 

So, last Thursday, my supervisor, Dave—who is usually a pretty laid-back guy, honestly, he’s been there for like fifteen years and nothing really fazes him—he actually had to pull me aside. He showed me this whole list of discrepancies in the sections I’d logged that morning. I had logged a shipment of hex bolts as carriage bolts, and I completely skipped over a whole pallet of washers because I got distracted trying to reorganize the shelving unit next to it. So now, I’m having to double-check everything with him. I literally have to take my logs to Dave before I can enter them into the system, which is just humiliating, honestly. I've been doing this job for a long time, and having to be micromanaged like that because I'm making stupid mistakes... it's really frustrating. But I just can't seem to slow down enough to catch the errors myself.

And then, on top of all that, things at home are just... tense. Really tense. With Tom being home all the time now because of his back, you'd think we'd be settling into this new routine, maybe treating it a bit like an early retirement, you know? Finding a rhythm. But instead, we are just constantly at each other's throats. Well, mostly me at his throat, if I'm being honest. Like I mentioned before, I just snap at him. We’ve been arguing so much over the smallest things—like him asking about the cabinets, or the landscaping ideas, or even just what we’re having for dinner. It's gotten to the point where it feels like we’re just walking on eggshells around each other. He’s trying to stay out of my way because he doesn't know when I'm going to explode, and I'm just irritated that he's even in the room breathing too loudly while I'm trying to figure out how to rewire the toaster. It's exhausting. It's not how I want us to be spending this time together at all, but I just can't seem to turn off this... this motor inside me that gets so aggravated when things aren't moving at my speed. So, yeah, it's definitely causing problems. Big ones.

inference.note: Confirmed manic symptoms (decreased sleep need, distractibility, irritability, grandiosity, goal-directed hyperactivity) causing significant impairment at work and home, with no psychotic features (no hallucinations/delusions) and no prior mood episodes. This supports a manic episode without psychotic symptoms, consistent with F30.1; F30.9 retained as a less specific fallback.

doctor.intent: Assess decreased need for sleep, a core manic symptom, to confirm full manic episode criteria (vs. subthreshold/unspecified presentation)
doctor.question: Over this past month, have you noticed that you need much less sleep than usual—like feeling fully rested after only a few hours—without feeling tired the next day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decreased need for sleep, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I know I said earlier about wanting to rebuild the garage at four in the morning, but that’s more just... me lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling fan, with my brain just racing and going over the blueprints in my head while I’m *trying* to sleep. It’s not like I actually function well if I only get a few hours. Goodness, no. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am absolutely dragging the next day. 

I've always been a real stickler for my sleep schedule, you know? Usually, I'm in bed by 10:00 PM, right after the local news—we always watch Channel 5 because Tom likes the weatherman, Greg, he says he's the only one who doesn't exaggerate the rain forecasts—and I usually sleep right through until my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM for work. Lately, though, with Tom tossing and turning so much because of his back pain, he keeps waking me up. He shifts around trying to get comfortable, the mattress squeaks, and then I'm awake. And once I'm awake, that motor just starts humming again and I can't shut it off. 

But I definitely still *need* the sleep. If I only get three or four hours because of all the tossing and turning, I feel like absolute garbage the next morning. I'm yawning all through my shift, having to drink three or four cups of that awful, burnt breakroom coffee just to keep my eyes open while I'm trying to go over my inventory logs with Dave. Even with all this weird, buzzy energy I've been having, my body still physically demands a full night's rest. If I don't get it, I might still be moving fast and snapping at people, but underneath it all, I'm just completely wiped out. So, no, I definitely don't feel fully rested on just a few hours. I wish I did, honestly, because I could get so much more done around the house, but no, I definitely still need my sleep.

inference.note: Sleep is preserved in need (she still requires 7-8 hours and feels exhausted without it, ruling out true decreased need for sleep) and there are no psychotic symptoms (denies hallucinations or true grandiose delusions). Combined with clear elevated/irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility, and significant impairment in work and relationship functioning over the past month, this fits a manic episode without psychotic symptoms, narrowing away from unspecified.
